## Identification and Estimation {#sec-estimation}

### What the Designed Variation Buys {#sec-est-variation}

<!--
TODO: prose. The substance, from the papers now read in full:

(a) POSITION ENTERS SEARCH COSTS, NOT UTILITY. @Ursu_2018 §4.3 enumerates all seven
ways position could act (on v, on epsilon, on c, and combinations) and rules out all
but c using three tests:
   - purchases conditional on click are unaffected by position -> rules out any case
     where position enters pre-search utility v (her Cases 1, 4, 5, 7);
   - consumers click TOP-ranked alternatives first -> rules out position acting on

   - an exogenous demotion (opaque offers) lowers clicks on the demoted hotel ->

We can run the first two natively and better: we randomize position in every task and
we observe click order directly, which she had to import from a companion data set.
The third we do not need, because our demotions ARE the design.
This is the argument that licenses putting position in Z and not in X. It should be
run and reported as a design check in every SIFT study, not assumed.

(b) SEPARATING PREFERENCES FROM SEARCH COSTS. @Morozov_2021 §4.3.2: stopping decisions
depend on the REALIZED utilities of already-searched alternatives but not on their
search costs, which are sunk. So trade xi against c holding the mean reservation value
z-bar fixed: search order is unchanged, but the higher intercept raises realized utility
and makes stopping more likely. Their Appendix D sharpens this into an observable
moment -- the RECALL RATE, the probability of purchasing an alternative searched
earlier in the sequence, responds to the intercept but NOT to search cost. We observe
recall directly (free recall, full click sequence), which makes this our cleanest
separation moment.

(c) WHAT THE PANEL BUYS, AND WHAT IT DOES NOT. @Morozov_2021 §4.3 proves nonparametric
identification of individual-level preferences AND search costs from panel search data,
but the argument assumes the number of sessions per consumer goes to infinity; with
2-35 sessions (mean 5) they estimate hyperparameters only, not individual parameters
(their §5.1). At T = 10 we should claim hierarchical posteriors in the conjoint
tradition, NOT nonparametric individual identification. Say this plainly.

(d) WHAT NEITHER PANEL NOR SHIFTER BUYS ALONE. @Morozov_2021 has the panel and still
normalizes sigma_epsilon, reporting that little variation in their data speaks to it
(their Appendix C); @Yavorsky_2021 has an exogenous shifter and no panel, and estimates
it. SIFT has both, and -- see @sec-model-setup -- part of the post-search variance is
fixed by the design rather than assumed. This is the sharpest version of the
identification claim and belongs in the introduction.

(e) SEARCH-COST LEVELS AND SPELL LENGTH. @Ursu_2018 §6.1 reports baseline search costs
above $102 and attributes the magnitude to observing one click per search impression
with no way to link a consumer's impressions; restricting to impressions with two or
more clicks cuts mean search costs by up to 83%. Single-spell data mechanically
inflates search costs. The panel is a levels argument, not only a heterogeneity
argument.

### Testing the Zero-Search-Cost Restriction {#sec-est-nesting}

<!--
TODO. IMPORTANT: the test cannot be a Wald test on the estimated search cost.
Zero is a limit rather than an interior point -- c -> 0 corresponds to g(c) -> +infinity
and log c -> -infinity -- so the null sits at a boundary in every parameterization.
Construct the test from observable implications instead:
   - holdout fit of SIFT against the nested conjoint model;
   - the observable implication itself (does anyone leave alternatives unopened);
   - a likelihood-ratio comparison with a simulated rather than chi-squared reference
     distribution.
Note also that this argues for estimating c rather than g directly, even though
estimating g avoids the root-find during optimization (@Ursu_Seiler_Honka_2024 §5.2).
-->

### Individual-Level Estimation from a Task Panel {#sec-est-panel}

<!--

   2. Two-stage empirical Bayes: estimate the hyperparameters by simulated maximum
      likelihood with importance sampling, then draw individual posteriors by
      Metropolis-Hastings conditional on the estimated hyperparameters. This is
      exactly what @Morozov_2021 do to compute personalized prices (their §7.2 and
      Appendix H), and it is far cheaper than full HB.

### Estimation {#sec-est-estimation}

<!--
TODO. Runtime is a binding practical constraint: a fit has to complete overnight, not
over a week. The four candidate simulators, with published timings:

  @Ursu_Seiler_Honka_2024 Table 2 (1,000 consumers, 5 sessions, 5 alternatives,
  heterogeneous):
    importance sampling    5h20m,  RMSE 0.01
    kernel-smoothed       29h48m,  RMSE 0.13  (+ ~32h to calibrate the scaling vector)
    GHK                  198h24m,  RMSE 0.09

  @Chung_2025 Table 1 (1,000 consumers, 5 alternatives + outside option,
  cross-sectional, 100 replications):
    their GHK-type simulator   0.48 min,  SSE 0.040   <- one to two orders faster
    kernel-smoothed            5-7 min,   SSE 0.21-2.98
    crude frequency           15-127 min, SSE ~0.11
    @Jiang_2021 pre-search-shock GHK  1.2-1.5 min, but needs a grid search over sigma_e

LEADING CANDIDATE: @Chung_2025. Three separate mechanisms make it fast, and all three
bite harder in our setting than in theirs:

  1. NO TUNING CONSTANTS. It computes actual probabilities rather than kernel-smoothed
     indicator violations, so there is no scaling vector to calibrate. That removes an
     entire pre-estimation stage -- @Ursu_Seiler_Honka_2024 Appendix B report ~32 hours
     for it -- and @Chung_2025 §6.3 show the stage cannot be shortcut, because on field
     data the maximized likelihood declines mechanically in the scaling factor, so
     calibration has to run through out-of-sample prediction instead.
  2. NO ROOT-FINDING IN THE INNER LOOP. Bounds on reservation values are obtained by
     evaluating g FORWARD on a utility difference -- closed form, vectorizable -- and
     g-inverse is needed only for the K search costs actually drawn, from a spline
     precomputed once before estimation (their footnote 7). With K << J, which is the
     SIFT regime, this is most of the work removed. Contrast the reference R code,
     which root-finds per alternative per respondent per likelihood evaluation.
  3. IT SCALES WELL IN J WHEN K IS SMALL. Unsearched alternatives enter as a product of
     closed-form cdf evaluations, one per alternative. This is the opposite of the
     kernel simulator's behaviour, where a large J-K adds smoothed penalty terms that
     come to dominate the objective (the smoothing-convention issue discussed above).

WHAT ADOPTING IT COMMITS US TO. Their simulator requires the stochastic component of the
reservation value to be the search cost rather than a pre-search taste shock
(@sec-model-setup). Consequences to verify in @sec-simstudy rather than assume:
  - sigma_epsilon. @Chung_2025 fix it at one, as everyone does. Our randomized position
    enters as the location parameter of the search-cost distribution -- exactly the
    shifted-exponential specification of their §6.2 -- so @Yavorsky_2021's shifter
    argument should apply, but nobody has estimated sigma_epsilon inside this simulator.
    This is the single most important thing the simulation study has to establish,
    because @sec-managerial depends on it.
  - Misspecification. Their Table 7 shows RATIOS of preference parameters are recovered
    correctly even when the randomness is put in the wrong place; their Table 6 shows
    LEVELS are not, and their search-cost levels swing wildly. Relative part-worths are
    safe; monetized search costs are not. Say so.
  - Estimate both specifications on the same simulated data and report the comparison.

THE ONE PIECE THAT ALREADY EXISTS FOR US. @Chung_2025 Appendix B.4 works out the case
where the outside option's utility is known prior to search, so respondents who click
nothing are representable in the likelihood, and shows parameter recovery for it. That
is SIFT's no-click exit, and it is the only treatment of it in the four reference
implementations.

CONFLICTING EVIDENCE ON IMPORTANCE SAMPLING, to resolve before relying on either:
@Morozov_2021 Appendix G and @Ursu_Seiler_Honka_2024 Table 2 both find importance
sampling fast and accurate; @Chung_2025 Table 3 find it badly biased -- heterogeneity
standard deviations collapse and preference means shrink most of the way to zero. The
likely explanation is resourcing rather than a defect: @Chung_2025 give it 100^2 draws
per observation where @Morozov_2021 use up to 10^6, and importance sampling is acutely
sensitive to the proposal density, which @Morozov_2021 centre on moment-matched starting
values and @Chung_2025 do not describe. Worth settling in the simulation study, since
importance sampling remains the fallback.

PANEL AND HETEROGENEITY. The per-task likelihood contributions multiply across tasks with
no structural change. For individual-level output, @Chung_2025 Appendix B.5 run their
simulator inside a Metropolis-within-Gibbs sampler and compare against the Bayesian
approach of @Morozov_2023, which they find biased and no faster.

ORDER OF WORK: aggregate first (it validates against the reference implementations), then
heterogeneity, then HB. See @sec-appendix for the validation protocol.

STARTING VALUES. The effective-value representation of @Armstrong_2017 and @Choi_2018,
w = min(u, z), gives purchase probabilities in near-probit form
(@Ursu_Seiler_Honka_2024 §3.1). Too coarse to estimate from, but cheap enough to
generate starting values, which buys optimizer iterations.
